div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many real-time services are implemented as multiprocessors that handle a number of incoming aperiodic tasks. To guarantee certain response times for aperiodic tasks, we reject tasks that may not be able to meet their response times or could jeopardize the response time of other tasks. Previous results by Abdelzaher and Lu [1] provide a constant time schedulability test that can be used in admission control in uni-processors. The priority assigned to each aperiodic task is time independent, meaning that a certain task, with a certain relative deadline, will get the same priority independently when it arrives. This result was later generalized to global (non-partitioned) multiprocessor scheduling by Abdelzaher et al. [2]. The multiprocessor generalization is, however, restricted to a very limited type of tasks called liquid tasks.

Previous results on global multiprocessor scheduling of periodic tasks show that the deadline monotonic priority assignment scheme may lead to missed deadlines even if the multiprocessor utilization is very low. The reason for this is the so-called Dhall´s effect [5]. By assuming liquid task sets this problem is removed since liquid task sets do not suffer from Dhall´s effect, and the deadline monotonic priority assignment scheme is in fact optimal for such task sets. For more realistic task sets one must, however, consider Dhall´s effect. The state-of-the-art technique for doing priority assignment in such cases (for periodic tasks) is an algorithm developed initially by Andersson and Jonsson [4], and then improved by Lundberg [7]. Based on the task utilizations, this priority assignment algorithm groups tasks into two categories: light tasks and heavy tasks.

This priority assignment algorithm is in this paper adapted to aperiodic tasks. The optimal utilization threshold value defining a task as light or heavy is also provided, thus eliminating the need for further improvements of this state-of-the-art algorithm. The optimal threshold value also serves as a constant time utilization test that can be used in admission control.

div.head: Problem Definition and Previous Results
div.p: Consider a task model in which independent aperiodic tasks arrive at a multiprocessor-based real-time system at random without prior knowledge from the scheduler. The multiprocessor schedules the arrived tasks by arranging them in a single queue and dequeue them in priority order when a processor becomes available. We assume that a lower priority task may be preempted when a higher priority task arrives to the system. A preempted task is put back into the queue, and the task can later be restarted on any processor in the system. There is no penalty for switching from one task to another. We assume m identical processors, i.e. up to m tasks can be executing at the same time.

A task T i constitutes a single invocation, defined by an arrival time A i , an execution time C i , and a relative deadline D i . The absolute deadline is thus A i +D i . We also define a utilization U i for task T i such that

div.p: The maximal synthetic utilization for a task (arrival) pattern is denoted by US max = max t US(t).

Scheduling policies for aperiodic tasks can be classified as either time-independent or non-time-independent [1]. A scheduling policy is time-independent if the priority assigned to a task does not depend of its absolute arrival time. In our case, this means that the priority of task T i should be calculated from C i and D i .

It turns out that the well-known deadline monotonic priority assignment algorithm, which is optimal for the uni-processor and the partitioned multiprocessor cases, is not optimal using global multiprocessor scheduling. Fig. 1 shows the so-called Dhall's effect, i.e. the deadline monotonic priority assignment algorithm can result in missed deadlines even if the synthetic utilization is very low.

Dhall's effect [5] shows that a direct application of the deadline monotonic priority assignment scheme may result in failure to meet deadlines even for systems with very low multiprocessor utilization. Previous results on periodic tasks [3][7] show that the problems with Dhall's effect can be handled by dividing the tasks into two categories based on their utilization U i . Tasks for which U i > U threshold (m) are considered as heavy tasks, and are assigned the highest priority in the system (all tasks in this category have the same priority). Tasks for which U i • U threshold (m) are light tasks. For light tasks the highest priority is assigned to tasks with lowest D i , i.e. we use deadline monotonic priority assignment. The priority of a light task is, however, always less than the priority of a heavy task. In this paper we apply the same strategy to aperiodic tasks. We calculate a formula for the optimal utilization threshold U threshold (m) as a function of the number of processors m: We show that all task (arrival) patterns for which the synthetic utilization using m processors is always lower than or equal to U threshold (m) can be scheduled on m processors. We also show that this threshold is the best possible, thus eliminating the need for further research concerning the threshold value.

The quantity U threshold (m) plays two roles simultaneously. It is a threshold for the synthetic utilization in the admission control of incoming tasks, and it is a threshold for the categorization of light and heavy tasks.

div.head: Calculating the optimal U threshold (m)
div.p: We start by considering all tasks as light. We consider a multiprocessor server with m processors, receiving arbitrary (liquid and non-liquid) aperiodic tasks.

Among the set of task patterns, some are schedulable, and some are not schedulable. Our aim is to calculate a bound U bound so that all task patterns with US max • U bound are schedulable. In this paper we calculate the largest such bound possible within the problem formulation. This optimal U bound is denoted U threshold (m), where m is the number of processors.

Let a critically schedulable task pattern be a schedulable task pattern in which some task has zero slack, i.e. there are arbitrarily small perturbations of the task pattern, and of its maximal utilization US max , so the perturbed pattern is unschedulable. Within the set of such patterns, the worst-case critically schedulable task patterns are the task patterns where US max is minimal.
It follows that US max = U threshold (m) if US max is the maximal synthetic utilization for a worst-case critically schedulable task pattern.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We propose four different strategies. They give increasing server utilization, but they have increasing complexity: The admission test bound is based on the assumption that each heavy task occupies a processor of its own. If a (very) heavy task T i with a utilization of 2*U threshold (m) arrives to the system, it is therefore safe to only increase US(t) with U threshold (m)/m in the interval A i • t < A i +D i . This will reduce the synthetic utilization thus making it possible to accept more tasks. It is possible to compare the aperiodic and periodic cases. The problems with Dhall's effect are the same and the technique of dividing the task into light and heavy is a useful technique for avoiding this problem for the periodic as well as for the aperiodic case. The threshold values are, however, not the same. Table 1, compares the optimal threshold values for the periodic and the aperiodic cases. It turns out that the threshold values are somewhat lower in the aperiodic case. This is easy to understand since any periodic task set can be written as a set of aperiodic tasks. The opposite is, however, not true. In the aperiodic case we are thus looking for a minimum in a larger set of possible task patterns than in the periodic case. This is the reason why the values are lower in the aperiodic case.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have adapted a state-of-the-art priority assignment technique for periodic tasks [3][4] [7] to the aperiodic case. Based on the utilization of each task, the priority assignment algorithm groups tasks into two categories: light tasks and heavy tasks. A task is heavy if its utilization is above a certain threshold, otherwise the task is light.
The main contribution in this paper is the function for the optimal threshold value:

We obtain %. The quantity U threshold (m) plays two roles simultaneously. It is a threshold for the synthetic utilization in the admission control of incoming tasks, and it is a threshold for the categorization of light and heavy tasks. We have thus provided an optimal threshold for the state-of-the-art priority assignment algorithm for aperiodic tasks. As a consequence of this, we also provide the best fixed time admission control test known to us; the test is best in the sense that we are accepting a maximum number of tasks while still guaranteeing that all deadlines will be met.

The results generalize previous single-processor results [1] to multiprocessors, and extend previous multiprocessor results by considering arbitrary tasks and not only liquid tasks [2], which is a special case of our general formulas.

div.p: depending on the task set (the priority of T x ' is lower than the priority of T y '):

• T x ' is blocked waiting for T y '. In this case we know that the increase in the computation time of T y ' will affect the slack of T x ', and the theorem is thus true in this case. • T x ' is not blocked waiting for T y '. In this case we know that T x ' and T y ' execute in parallel. The reduction of the computation time of a task will thus affect at most one of T x ' and T y ', and the theorem is true in this case.

If there are three tasks T x ', T y ' and T z ' for which the computation time will increase we can separate three cases depending on the task set (the priority of T x ' is lower than the priority of T y ', and the priority of T y ' is lower than the priority of T z '):

• T x ' is blocked waiting for both T y ' and T z '. In this case we know that an increase of the execution time of T y ' and T z ' will affect the slack of T x ', and the theorem is true in this case. • No task for which the computation time will increase is blocked waiting for any other task for which the computation time will increase. In this case we know that the tasks for which the computation time will increase execute in parallel. The re-duction of the computation time of a task will thus affect at most one of the tasks for which the computation time will increase, and the theorem is thus true in this case. • One task for which the computation time will increase is blocked waiting for one other task for which the computation time will increase. In this case we know that the reduction of the computation time from a task affects (at most) either the third task for which the computation time will increase or the two other tasks. By combining the arguments above we see that the theorem is true also in this case.
The same way of arguing can be used for the cases when there are four, five, six,.. tasks for which the computation time will increase.

If we have a task set with a zero slack task and add some computation time to this task set there must be at least one of the non-zero slack tasks that will either still have zero slack or it will miss its deadline after the redistribution of computation time.
